title: Best States for Lottery Winners Taxes: $100M Breakdown
description: Win a $100M Powerball jackpot? Your take-home ranges from $29.8M in New York to $30M+ in Florida and Texas. See exact dollar figures by state.
content:
What This Article Calculates and Why Your State Address Costs You Millions

If you won a $100 million Powerball jackpot tonight — say, a ticket matching last Saturday's draw of 12, 13, 24, 32, 35 + PB 11 — the advertised number on the screen is not what lands in your bank account. Not even close. The IRS takes a large cut first. Then your state government takes its share. And the difference between winning in the right state versus the wrong one can mean more than $4 million in additional tax you never see.

This article calculates exactly what a $100 million Powerball jackpot pays out in five major states — California, Texas, Florida, New York, and New Jersey — using real tax rates and real dollar figures at every step. For personalized estimates based on your actual jackpot size, use our lottery tax calculator. But if you want to understand the mechanics and the state-by-state differences right now, keep reading.

Lump Sum vs. Annuity — The Numbers You Start With on a $100M Jackpot

The first decision every jackpot winner faces is whether to take the annuity or the lump sum cash option. This choice determines the starting number for all tax calculations.

The Annuity Option

The annuity pays the full $100,000,000 advertised jackpot over 30 annual payments, each increasing by approximately 5% per year. Your first payment would be roughly $1,505,000, rising to over $6,000,000 by the final installment. Each annual payment is taxed as ordinary income in the year received, keeping you in the top federal bracket every year.

The Lump Sum Cash Option

The lump sum cash value for a $100 million jackpot is approximately $47,600,000 — about 47.6% of the advertised prize. This is the present-value equivalent the lottery commission holds in its prize account. Every tax calculation below uses this $47,600,000 lump sum as the starting point, because that is the number most winners actually choose and the number that produces the sharpest state-to-state comparisons.

Federal Tax Calculation — What the IRS Takes First

Federal taxes apply identically regardless of which state you live in. The IRS treats lottery winnings as ordinary income, and a $47.6 million lump sum pushes you deep into the top marginal bracket.

Step 1: Federal Withholding

The lottery operator withholds 24% immediately before cutting your check. On a $47,600,000 lump sum, that withholding equals $11,424,000. You receive a check for roughly $36,176,000 — but you are not done with the IRS yet.

Step 2: Top Marginal Rate at Tax Time

The 37% top federal marginal rate applies to income above $626,350 for single filers in 2025. Since your entire lump sum far exceeds that threshold, the effective federal tax rate on the bulk of your winnings is 37%. Applied to the full $47,600,000, that is $17,612,000 in total federal income tax. Subtract the $11,424,000 already withheld, and you owe an additional $6,188,000 when you file your return.

What Remains After Federal Tax

After federal taxes at the full 37% rate, your $47,600,000 lump sum shrinks to approximately $29,988,000. That is roughly $30 million left before your state gets involved. This calculation assumes single-filer status, no deductions, and no other income sources. Your actual federal liability will vary.

State-by-State Tax Breakdown — California, Texas, Florida, New York, and New Jersey

This is where the best states for lottery winners taxes question gets answered in hard dollar figures. Every calculation below starts from the same $29,988,000 post-federal baseline.

California — $0 State Tax on Lottery Winnings

California lottery taxes on lottery prizes are unique: California does not tax lottery winnings at the state level. Despite having one of the highest income tax rates in the country (up to 13.3%), lottery prizes are specifically exempt under California law. State tax owed: $0. Take-home after all taxes: $29,988,000.

Texas — $0 State Tax on Lottery Winnings

Texas has no state income tax at all. Lottery winners in Texas pay federal taxes and nothing else to any state authority. State tax owed: $0. Take-home after all taxes: $29,988,000.

Florida — $0 State Tax on Lottery Winnings

Florida also has no state income tax. A Powerball winner claiming a ticket purchased in Florida pays only federal taxes. State tax owed: $0. Take-home after all taxes: $29,988,000.

New Jersey — 8% State Tax on Lottery Winnings

New Jersey taxes lottery winnings above $10,000 at a flat rate of 8% for prizes up to $500,000, but winners of large jackpots are subject to New Jersey's top income tax rate of 10.75% for income over $1 million. Applied to the $47,600,000 lump sum, New Jersey's top rate produces a state tax bill of approximately $5,117,000. Take-home after all taxes: approximately $24,871,000.

New York — 8.82% State Tax Plus City Tax

New York lottery taxes are among the highest in the nation. The state levies 8.82% on lottery winnings, and winners who live in New York City face an additional city income tax of up to 3.876%. For a state-only calculation on the $47,600,000 lump sum: New York state tax equals approximately $4,198,000. That alone drops your take-home to roughly $25,790,000. Add New York City tax of approximately $1,844,000 and NYC residents keep only about $23,946,000 — more than $6 million less than winners in no-tax states.

The difference between winning a $100M Powerball jackpot in New York City vs. Florida is over $6,000,000 in take-home pay — on the exact same jackpot, the exact same lump sum, the exact same federal tax bill.

State Rankings — Best to Worst for Lottery Winner Take-Home Pay

Across all U.S. states, the best states for lottery winners taxes fall into clear tiers. Here is how the full national picture ranks:

Tier 1 — No State Tax on Lottery Winnings (Best)

  • California — Lottery-specific exemption; no state tax on prizes
  • Florida — No state income tax
  • Texas — No state income tax
  • Washington — No state income tax
  • Wyoming — No state income tax
  • South Dakota — No state income tax
  • Tennessee — No state income tax on wages or prizes
  • New Hampshire — No state income tax on lottery winnings
  • Pennsylvania — State law exempts lottery winnings from state income tax

Tier 2 — Moderate State Tax (Middle Ground)

  • Most remaining states fall in the 3% to 6% range, costing winners between $1.4 million and $2.9 million in additional state tax on a $47.6 million lump sum

Tier 3 — High State Tax (Worst)

  • New York — 8.82% state rate plus up to 3.876% city tax for NYC residents
  • New Jersey — Up to 10.75% on large jackpots
  • Oregon — 8% state lottery tax
  • Minnesota — Up to 9.85% on high income

That is not a rounding error — it is a house, several cars, and years of investment returns.
